newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Contaminated food takes heavy toll -WHO report.
newsitem.headline: Contaminated food takes heavy toll -WHO report.

text.p: Hundreds of millions of people fall victim each year to diseases like cholera and salmonella after eating contaminated food, the World Health Organisation said on Wednesday.
But the United Nations agency said foodborne diseases were vastly under-reported, especially by developing countries, or by authorities fearing an outbreak will damage tourism and trade.

"It is estimated that the reported incidence of foodborne diseases represents less than 10 per cent, or maybe even less than one per cent of the real incidence," the WHO said in its World Health Statistics Quarterly.
"Surveys in a few countries indicate that foodborne diseases may be 300-350 times more frequent than the reported cases tend to indicate," it added, without naming the countries.
In industrialised nations, parasites and emerging pathogens present in animals but not visible at slaughter pose a challenge to the food industry and health authorities, the WHO said.
Japan and Scotland, where the E.coli bacterium caused a rash of deaths last year, are among countries where cases are on the increase.
Foodborne bacteria and viruses commonly cause mild gastro-intestinal illness, but two to three percent of patients develop complications such as heart or respiratory problems.
Outbreaks take their toll not only on victims, but also on the economy, according to the 154-page study.

In the United States alone, seven foodborne pathogens found in animal products cause 3.3 million-12.3 million cases and 3,900 deaths each year, two U.S. Department of Agriculture experts wrote in an article in the report.
They calculated the annual cost of human illness at $6.5 billion to $34.9 billion.

"However, these estimates undervalue true societal costs, because they focus on medical costs and productivity losses and omit or do not fully include valuations of other costs to individuals (such as psychological costs), costs to industry or costs to the public sector," said the authors, Jean Buzby and Tanya Roberts.

People who eat greater quantities of food likely to contain pathogens or prefer raw or rare animal protein products -- such as cheeses made of unpasteurised milk -- raw shellfish, raw or rare meat products and many egg dishes, are at higher risk, they added.
The WHO called on authorities in its 191 member states to enforce food safety laws and improve reporting.
To illustrate the scale of the problem, the Geneva-based agency said 1.5 billion children worldwide aged under five get diarrhoea each year, resulting in more than three million deaths.
"...a significant proportion of the diarrhoeal disease cases are foodborne in origin," Fritz Kaeferstein, director of the WHO's programme of food safety and food aid, said in the report.

Diarrhoeal diseases -- particularly in infants or children -- and cholera have traditionally been perceived as waterborne or as being transmitted by humans, he wrote. However, weaning food has often been contamined with pathogens.

Foodborne diseases are often misdiagnosed and wrongly treated, especially when the illness is of a new type unknown to health workers, Kaeferstein said. Diarrhoea may be blamed on teething, indigestion or spicy foods.
In addition to difficulties in diagnosis, some countries fear the negative effects of publicising an outbreak of a foodborne disease, the WHO said.

"Concern about the possibility of food exports being rejected and/or loss of tourism have been a disincentive for many governments to release information on foodborne disease epidemics," said Kaeferstein.
